name: Day
funFact: Earth's day is getting longer by about 1.8 milliseconds per century due to tidal friction from the Moon. 350 million years ago a day was only 22 hours and there were 400 days in a year. The oldest evidence of this comes from fossilised coral growth rings, which record daily cycles and reveal more rings per year the further back you go in geological time.

name: Hour
funFact: The 24-hour day was established by ancient Egyptians, who divided daylight into 10 hours plus 2 twilight hours. Mechanical clocks only became accurate enough to track individual minutes in the 1600s — before that, a clock with a minute hand was considered a showpiece rather than a tool. The first clock with a minute hand was built by Jost Bürgi around 1577.

name: Minute
funFact: The 60-minute hour traces back to Babylonian mathematics, which used base-60 because 60 has 12 divisors — making it unusually divisible into thirds, quarters, fifths, and sixths without fractions. Base-10 only has four divisors. We still use base-60 for time and angles, 4,000 years after the Babylonians chose it for purely practical arithmetic reasons.

name: Second
funFact: The second was originally 1/86,400 of a mean solar day — but Earth's rotation is gradually slowing. Since 1967 it has been defined by atomic clocks as exactly 9,192,631,770 oscillations of a caesium-133 atom. This is so precise that atomic clocks lose less than one second over 300 million years — yet we still add 'leap seconds' periodically to keep clocks aligned with the slowing Earth.
